lxc_489a2b35e7373f28.text: Understanding timing, business cycles, selling, and opportunity cost can help you see what each financial choice gives up.

lxc_73b71a7eccb0a2b4.text: An economy does not grow at the same speed all the time.

lxc_27ee3448f1a6f4ab.text: A **business cycle** is the longer pattern of growth and slowdown.

lxc_899fe841219b6b08.text: The NBER, a US research group, records these cycles by marking peaks and troughs.

lxc_2240c3e5d6a05033.text: A peak is a high point, and a trough is a low point.

lxc_bf13c43297717e83.text: An **expansion** runs from a trough to a peak, as economic activity grows.

lxc_04754739b7d8df41.text: A **recession** runs from a peak to a trough, as activity falls.

lxc_6b7962b2c79c7efa.text: The NBER says expansion is the normal state and most recessions are brief.

lxc_fab3fbdd5f38a952.text: This longer view matters because one bad market day does not describe the whole economy.

lxc_d2e7a3afb72899ac.text: When thinking about timing, first ask whether you are seeing daily noise or a wider economic change.

lxc_7186b93c2926a964.text: **Trading** usually means trying to benefit from shorter price moves.

lxc_d7a2bbb1aa844cd1.text: A trader may buy and sell often.

lxc_58ad1e443aefff74.text: **Investing** usually means owning something for longer, so growth and compounding have time to work.

lxc_5c2bcdfcaf48f2c0.text: Both traders and investors sell, but their reasons and time periods may be different.

lxc_12a270481de7a773.text: Selling is therefore not the opposite of investing.

lxc_9b8c91bacd1fd760.text: It is one action inside a larger plan.

lxc_9684b8b322401b03.text: The important questions are why you are selling and what happens next.

lxc_438ddb2f300a35d2.text: Market timing needs two successful decisions: leaving before a fall and returning before a rise.

lxc_585edbe83da378df.text: The Bank of Singapore explains that most people get one or both decisions wrong.

lxc_0ef94e93a66cb403.text: A person may sell during fear, then wait too long while prices recover.

lxc_74ab5d50449e0675.text: **Market timing** means trying to buy and sell at perfect moments.

lxc_1c800f9481903de5.text: Charles Schwab studied five hypothetical investors.

lxc_ce83e439df9c78be.text: Each received $2,000 every year for 20 years ending in 2024, and the study tracked the S&P 500, an index of large US companies.

lxc_e2c912a212aece7f.text: Investing on the first trading day of each year finished near $170,555, only about $15,522 less.

lxc_9605eff1c6ab6a56.text: Regular fixed investments, called **dollar-cost averaging**, finished near $166,591.

lxc_6f52a86805e94710.text: Even the worst yearly timing beat staying in cash, which ended near $47,357.

lxc_e3a1cb1a6d7a3bfa.text: Across 80 rolling 20-year periods going back to 1926, investing immediately almost never finished last.

lxc_6b8dbe3a9f8bbec1.text: The example suggests that waiting for a perfect entry can have a high cost.

lxc_669a91c880b66dc8.text: **Time in the market** means staying invested over long periods instead of repeatedly trying to find perfect buying and selling days.

lxc_3cf24be650ff1c99.text: This can feel difficult during a sharp fall.

lxc_2ae0fb6907f01e09.text: However, strong market days often happen close to very weak ones.

lxc_66a12e7dca8b3663.text: RBC looked at market history back to 1973.

lxc_0da78a7ecc7016f3.text: Missing only the 10 most profitable trading days cut returns to about half compared with staying invested over that long period.

lxc_ddfe93364627cb6e.text: A shorter example showed the same timing problem.

lxc_0d1c8f79b09d538d.text: In 2023 through August, the S&P 500 was up nearly 18%.

lxc_99f3c5f92c3fdc8e.text: An investor who missed the 10 best days had losses instead.

lxc_78e549631667108c.text: If someone sells during fear and holds cash, the recovery may begin before that person feels ready to return.

lxc_4f0de22f9efc350b.text: **Compounding** happens when earlier growth can produce more growth.

lxc_9f4105e9984c85f2.text: It becomes more powerful as time passes, so time is not simply a background detail.

lxc_4b22df3ee8aff50e.text: It is part of how long-term investing works.

lxc_8f99290d234a892a.text: The Bank of Singapore used a simple illustration of $100 growing at 8% for 20 years.

lxc_51ebcde884bbe254.text: It compared compound growth with simple returns.

lxc_c48d55d4df412373.text: At first, the difference was small.

lxc_dfd4aa9be2724321.text: Later, it grew wider, reaching about $206 by year 20 in the illustration.

lxc_b5aae7beff1827dd.text: The bank also compared $100 in the S&P 500 from 1970 through 2024.

lxc_14306d3a123d1129.text: Staying fully invested produced a very different result from missing the best 1% of weeks.

lxc_1a5bbd008253e38f.text: This does not make every short fall unimportant.

lxc_4f1515b1c3b14b68.text: It shows why short-term noise is not the whole story.

lxc_1552ac6c47bee058.text: **Opportunity cost** is the next-best use of money or time that you give up when you choose something.

lxc_d2c8c76dd7214c00.text: An OpenStax example asks you to imagine that a burger costs the same as four bus tickets.

lxc_6e65d336a93d5ad8.text: The real cost of the burger includes the four trips you can no longer take.

lxc_a65420e91ca2aaa8.text: The same lens works for investing: look at the choice, the alternative, and the result.

lxc_55cc1cebcfb3f6cf.text: Cash can provide patience and flexibility, but money left outside the market gives up the chance to grow.

lxc_eee834f865145b32.text: Selling can remove you from a possible fall, but it can also remove you from a sudden recovery.

lxc_1dfdfcdf457fd291.text: The earlier studies do not promise that every investment will rise.

lxc_78c17ec0676f44ca.text: They show why “doing nothing yet” is still a decision with a trade-off.
